The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Cote (Langelier) that Bill C-91, an Act to establish the Competition Tribunal and to amend the Combines Investigation Act and the Bank Act and other Acts in consequence thereof, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.

Mr. Speaker, I take great pleasure in resuming the debate on Bill C-91. I would like to preface my remarks by indicating to you, as have other members of my Party, that we intend to support Bill C-91 in principle at second reading. We do so despite some misgivings about areas where we feel the Bill could be improved. We do so as well because we happen to believe, contrary to the belief of my colleagues to my left in the New Democratic Party, given the historical development and the difficulty we have had in getting any kind of competition Bill through the House of Commons, that this Bill is better legislation than that which exists today to protect the consumers in the country.
Given that caveat, Mr. Speaker, we are prepared to support the Bill in principle. I do, however, wish to speak on certain parts to which the Liberal Party believes it can move amendments in committee, to improve the legislation. We hope we will be listened to by the Government.
I believe that since the Hon. Judy Erola, previously the Member of Parliament for Nickel Belt, introduced the last competitions Bill, the current Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Cote) has done a reasonable job of consultation and has put forward amendments which I believe will improve the legislation. With regard to those improvements, Mr. Speaker, the Bill differs from the previous Bill in that problems with corporate takeovers will be referred to a tribunal rather than the court system. I believe that is a significant improvement. I understand it was the Consumer's Association of Canada which recommended to the Government that the tribunal system replace the court system for appeals. I believe that that in itself is an improvement to the legislation.
I also believe very strongly, Mr. Speaker, that appointing lay members to the tribunal will be a step forward.
Order, please. Could I ask Members to hold their meetings somewhere else, out of respect for the Hon. Member who has the floor?

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I want to speak about the improvements to the Bill because 1 think they are fundamental to the reason the Liberal Party will support the Bill in principle at second reading. I firmly believe that the tribunal system is an improvement over the previous legislation. The
April 8, 1986

tribunal system will allow, for the first time, lay members to be appointed to ensure that consumer voices are heard when these matters are discussed.
Another improvement in the legislation is that Part VII matters have been removed from criminal jurisdiction and are now a matter of civil liability. That in itself is an improvement because restrictive trade practices and anti-competitive behaviour would then only require proof "on the balance of probabilities" as opposed to the criminal burden of "beyond a reasonable doubt". I believe that having it under criminal jurisdiction in previous legislation was a detriment to the ability of the inspectors within the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs to successfully charge corporations with violations, or restrictive trade practices.
Before I continue in a general way to outline some of our other concerns, it is important to note that Bill C-91 is before us to ensure, first and foremost, that free competition exists in the country. That is a very important principle. Second, the interest of consumers would be protected by this legislation. A third major and probably very controversial point, Mr. Speaker, is the achievement of economic efficiency. A number of speakers have already taken part in this debate. They have spoken about the need for maintaining free competition, the need to prevent abuses of economic power-in other words to protect the consumer-and the paramount need, in terms of our legislative program, to achieve economic efficiency in the economy.
I know that some Members have indicated previously that they find it odd that the five big lobby groups in the country have had a significant impact on previous legislation. Speaker after speaker has indicated that previous Governments have had difficulty passing any legislation with respect to competition because the lobby groups have been very successful in putting forth their viewpoints. Consumers have been very difficult to motivate in terms of lobby groups and, as a result, the weighting has been more on the side of big business than on that of the consumer. That fact is pointed to as one of the major reasons that previous Governments have failed to pass a competition Bill with objectives similar to those outlined in Bill C-91.
I do not find that surprising, Mr. Speaker. We in this House are not political virgins. We recognize that lobby groups are involved in every piece of legislation that comes before Parliament. I have no dispute with the big five, which includes the Canadian Manufacturers Association, the Business Council on National Issues, and the Canadian Chamber of Commerce. They have done the job which lobbyists are expected to do. It is our job, as Parliamentarians, to take into consideration the testimony given to the committee. We must also listen to the viewpoints expressed by other interest groups in the country. That is part and parcel of the political process in the country.
My colleagues to the left in the New Democratic Party have chastised some members of my Party on some of their interventions. They have asked why the Liberal Government
Competition Tribunal Act
was unable to get certain pieces of legislation through the House of Commons. It sounds to me like they are political virgins, that they are surprised that lobby groups have that degree of power.
When the Liberal Government brought in its Budget in November of 1981, through which we were attempting to make the tax system more equitable, the then Minister of Finance told our caucus to expect a great deal of pressure from lobby groups. He indicated that as a result of that Budget of 1981 one million more Canadians would have more disposable income in their hands. In other words, the Budget of 1981 was going to beneficially affect one million Canadians, and only approximately 225,000 Canadians would be adversely affected by that Budget.
Being a neophyte in the political arena, it came as a bit of a surprise to me that not one of the one million Canadians who would benefit from the legislation bothered to phone me as a Member of Parliament. However, I can assure you that all of the 225,000 Canadians being adversely affected by the legislation made sure that their views were made known to the Liberal caucus.
I recall very clearly, Mr. Speaker, that when it came time to vote on that Budget, through which we were attempting to rectify inequities in the tax system, my colleagues in the New Democratic Party consistently voted with the 225,000 Canadians who lobbied hard to reverse a number of major measures in that Budget. It therefore comes as a surprise to me today that the New Democratic Party is now pointing to the Liberal Party and chatising it for its inability to progress with competition policy.
I want to speak for a few moments on the principle of economic efficiency. That in itself is a laudable goal of any competition policy. Perhaps it is at the heart of the debate which will take place here regarding the Imasco takeover of Genstar. But more importantly, it allows us to raise the issue of other takeovers which have created a great deal of concentration of ownership of questionable value to the public interest. That is at the heart of the issue of achieving economic efficiency.
There are many in this country opposed to the Government intervening in corporate takeovers. The basis for their objection is that if Canadian conglomerates are going to compete in an international economy, they will have to do so with the same financial clout as the other players. In other words, as the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) pointed out this morning, it hinges upon the degree of integration that our economic system has with its American counterpart. It also raises the question of the extent to which we can use Government intervention to prevent corporate concentration from the standpoint of taxation.
As you know, the integration between the Canadian and American tax systems plays an integral part in corporate

April 8, 1986
Competition Tribunal Act
decision-making in North America. The Canadian tax system cannot be completely out of whack with the American system when it comes to allowing conglomerates on either side of the border taking over other conglomerates. We will have to distinguish between the non-financial corporate takeover of a financial institution from other takeovers in which financial institutions are not involved.
For example, let us go back to the takeover of Northern Telecom by Bell Telephone. There were those who argued that the degree of corporate concentration would not be in the public interest. I would argue that to some extent each one of these takeovers has to be judged on its own merit. That is why I am pleased to see that the Government has introduced the principle of a tribunal review. My argument is that that kind of corporate takeover was beneficial to the public interest because it created a company which is recognized world-wide as a leader in its field. As a result of that merger, Canadians have achieved some supremacy in the field of communications, which supremacy would not have been achieved had that takeover been prevented by Government legislation.
On the other hand, I have serious misgivings about some of the other corporate takeovers in this country. I am not now talking about the Genstar and Imasco deal, I am talking about takeovers involving two non-financial institution conglomerates. For example, last summer's takeover of Gulf Canada by Olympia & York. I do not disagree with the accounting principles used by Olympia & York. Frankly, they are doing what every other Canadian company does every day, and it is legal. However, that takeover cost the taxpayers $1 billion in foregone tax revenue, and not one job was created.
That is the kind of takeover this legislation will cover and justifiably so. That kind of takeover should go before the tribunal. It should be ascertained whether or not the public interest is being served. That is where I find fault with this legislation to some extent. In more cases than not there is no specific clause in the legislation which will allow class action suits to take place. There is nothing in the legislation which will allow a determination of whether the public interest is being served.
As another example we have the latest attempt by Olympia & York to purchase Hiram Walker. Whether or not they are successful remains to be seen. Hiram Walker, in an attempt to get around the bid by Olympia & York, is attempting to divest itself of its liquor business. The point I am making is that under this proposed legislation it would not be possible for that deal to be referred to the tribunal to determine whether or not it makes good sense for the workers involved in Windsor. This is the kind of thing that I believe should be added to the Bill.
As I indicated, I hope we can get this legislation through and into committee as quickly as possible. I hope members of the committee will view the representations made by various interested groups and Members of the Opposition to enhance the ability of the tribunal to look at corporate takeovers from the point of view of whether or not they serve the public interest.
I have indicated as well that I have some concern about the degree of corporate concentration of ownership in Canada over the last 15 to 20 years. I must share part of the blame, I suppose, if there is blame to be attached. However, whether it is a Conservative Government or a Liberal Government matters little. The point is that whenever we talk about corporate concentration, the argument is made for the need for integration of the tax system here and in the U.S. That argument was made when we were in power and it is being made now that the Conservatives are in power. It seems to me there is some validity to the argument.
I do not believe we live in a self-contained world. The tax system here has implications for foreign investment and foreign takeovers. The Hon. Member for Mississauga South properly pointed out that prior to 1970, when U.S. companies purchased Canadian entities, the interest on the money they borrowed to do so could be deducted from income from other sources. Yet Canadian corporations were not allowed the same benefit in Canada. As a result, up until 1970 we had ever-increasing foreign ownership of key sectors of our economy. That led to the pressure to change the tax laws to allow Canadian companies the same tax privileges as those in the U.S. We could then have Canadian conglomerates becoming larger and larger. To some extent I think that has been beneficial for the Canadian economy.
However, there has to be a public debate on how we are going to prevent abuse of corporate concentration of power, compatible with a tax system which we all recognize has to be integrated with that of the U.S. I would point out that in Canada at present 100 of the largest corporations control more than 50 per cent of the business assets. In the U.S. it is only roughly 30 per cent. So the concentration of power issue in Canada is of paramount importance, and we still do not address it in this legislation. Yet it will become of increasing importance, particularly when we have six or seven families in Canada who control the majority of the assets of the corporations listed on Canadian stock exchanges. That I hope can be addressed in committee, and with that I will entertain questions.

Mr. Speaker, it is with a great deal of interest that I rise today to speak to Bill C-91. We welcome this Bill. Its main quality is that it is better than the present almost non-existent legislation dealing with competition. As my hon. colleague just said, the incredible concentration of power now in the hands of six or seven families is of serious and ongoing concern. It is rhetorical to ask wehther do we need this piece of legislation. It is timely because of the number of mergers taking place across this country in the past year or so. Such a concentration of power in the hands of too few is counterproductive for most Canadians.
April 8, 1986

Competition is a vital key to the private sector and the private enterprise system. Some economists tell us that the more competition in the market-place the better it is for everyone because prices are lower due to the wide variety of choice of firms producing the same or similar types of products. This makes for better competition. Small business, provided it can face the competition, as it must, can assume its special position in the market. The challenge, with the innovation it brings, can lead to improved products and services, as well as keep the competition on its toes. This will in the long run benefit all of us-the consumer-that is you and me. In other words, the consumer benefits from lower prices and the wide range and variety of products available. On the other hand, when there is little competition product choice is restricted and prices are generally high.
I remember the sugar fiasco we all lived through. We went into the store and took a bag of sugar off the shelf. By the time we looked at the price and got to the checkout counter the price had gone up and we had to pay more.
Consumers and small businesses suffer the most from restricted trade and restricted competition. In a few moments I will give some examples of how the concentration of ownership has caused problems for a sector of the cultural industry, leading inevitably to a lack of ability to compete. This is not an esoteric subject, this is quotidian for monsieur et madame; it is tout-le-monde. What we are discussing here is a restraint through competition which leads to a restraint of selfexpression on the part of hundreds and hundreds, perhaps thousands of talented and creative Canadians in a wide variety of fields.
Essentially what we do is take the food out of their mouths. Most certainly we shrink their take-home pay when we have a high concentration and lack of competition in the field of cultural enterprises-artists, musicians, singers, sound and light technicians, film and script writers, stage and screen actors, producers, people iwth diversified jobs. That is what we are talking about and that is what competition in the cultural industrial field is all about.
Small entrepreneurs create the bulk of jobs that exist in Canada. We have an obligation to encourage and protect competition and fair trade practices to ensure the best conditions for an active, healthy market-place. The Liberal Party will be looking for indications that small business is protected from unfair competition by Bill C-91.
Let us look at competition in the film industry. The vertical integration of distribution and ownership concentration in the Canadian film industry has a severe negative impact on competition in this country, because it restricts trade andpre-vents entry into the Canadian market. The showcasing through our theatre screens is thereby limited, because "Distribution determines who can see what, when and how", to quote a report from the film industry task force.
As a result a special relationship between distributors and exhibitors in the 1920s large American studios were able to
Competition Tribunal Act
take control of the Canadian market, and things have not changed very much since then. An inquiry into these exclusive relationships in the film industry reached the following conclusions: That a combine exists in the motion picture industry in Canada within the meaning of the Combines Investigation Act; and that a combine exists and has existed at least since the year 1926. It is also felt that the combine has operated and is likely to operate to the detriment of the interests of the public.
The commissioner identified the members of the combine as Famous Players and the distributors, Paramount, Universal, Fox, Columbia, RKO, Warner, First National and a few others. He concluded that by reason of agreements, arrangements and other activities of the above mentioned, Famous Players in this instance has been able to acquire, particularly in the large cities and towns in Canada where the most profitable business is, such substantial control as to reduce competition to a minimum, making it extremely difficult for the independent theatres to survive. Booking arrangements have been restricted by the pooling and operating agreements and acquisitions I have just mentioned.
Canadian law at the time provided no remedy. Not much has changed since then, regretfully. Canadian law as early as 1930 demonstrated no apparent concern about the lack of open competition in Canada's film industry. We addressed this issue again in 1982, and I will have more to say about that in a moment.
Our neighbour to the south had the same situation with concentration of distribution. The United States Supreme Court decided in 1948, under the Sherman Act, that it was contrary to the public interest to have direct or indirect control over American theatre networks by these companies. The Supreme Court subsequently forced the five vertically integrated distribution companies-Paramount, Twentieth Century Fox, Loew's, which is now MGM, RKO and Warner Brothers-to divest themselves of all interest in film exhibition. In order to reduce ownership concentration in exhibition, the five had to give up about 1,200 of the 1,300 theatres they directly or indirectly controlled. As a result of that judgment, competition intensified at all levels, and the creativity and performance of the American film industry improved substantially. I think we could look forward to the same thing here. It is an unfortunate fact that the American action has not had any influence in Canada. This is just an overview or simplification of the major areas of concern for our cultural industries.
In 1982 the Cineplex Corporation, a Canadian theatrical chain, lodged a complaint with the Restrictive Trade Practices Commission. Cineplex alleged that seven of the large distributors operating in Canada had concluded long-term contracts under which they were committed to furnishing films to the two largest theatre chains, that is Odeon and Famous Players, excluding Cineplex and other companies. In other words the showcase was cut off and we had a restrictive trade practice, a cutting back of competition.

Competition Tribunal Act
As a result of the allegation, negotiations took place. An agreement was reached with the distributors to modify their distribution practices to "allow exhibitors to compete for each film". Following a decision of the Restrictive Trade Practices Commission under Section 31.2 of the Combines Investigation Act we got the commitment to modify the distribution practices and allow for the present "open bidding" system. In fact the report of the film industry task force, which reported to our Minister of CommunicationsfMr. Masse) in December, did not find that "open bidding" had really begun or was really truly working.
Let us consider Cineplex, as an example. In January of this year France Film lodged a complaint to the director of the Restrictive Trade Practices Commission stating that open bidding has not been the practice and that the 1982 agreement has been broken.

-Mr. Speaker, I draw your attention to this article published in La Presse of Thursday, January 16, 1986 under the heading: "France Film attack against Odeon and United Cinemas":
Yesterday the France Film cinema chain Filed a request with the Canadian Restrictive Trade Practices Commission in an attempt to put a stop to unfair competition from Cineplex-Odeon and United Cinemas. France Film President Pierre Rene stated that "we were often among the highest bidders last fall, yet we failed to get any of the films we wanted to have".
"We are convinced that Cineplex and Famous Players, a Gulf and Western subsidiary-
-and we in the House know all about Gulf and Western-
-and parent company of United Cinemas, did obtain copies of the films they wanted without even bidding, or by submitting lower bids than we did-
France Film, which supplies the Saint-Denis and Desjardins Complex cinemas as well as the Cinema de Paris in Quebec City and Sherbrooke among others- all told 30-odd cinemas in Quebec-was unable to obtain any of these American films-
At issue here was a matter of money, a loss of income at the most crucial time of the year, the winter holiday season-
We are still awaiting an answer from the Restrictive Trade Practices Commission on the complaint lodged by France Film. Hon. Members in this House probably do not realize the intensity and seriousness of the problem of concentration in the Canadian film industry. I can say the same for many of the sectors of the cultural industries which are big business. In 1985 in Canada there are still only two major theatre chains, Odeon-Cineplex with 472 screens and Famous Players with 471 screens. Together, they take in over 60 per cent of box office receipts. Each theatre chain is vertically integrated with a distributor. Famous Players and Paramount are both owned by the same conglomerate, Gulf and Western. Cineplex-Odeon is associated with Pan-Canadian and Universal through its MCA interests.
Any distributor vertically integrated with either of the major theatre chains can use this access to the main points of sale to acquire all commercially valuable foreign or domestic movies. As a result, other Canadian distributors' access to the major theatre chains is decidedly limited. By controlling distribution of the most lucrative productions, the company consolidates its position as an exhibitor, it is in a position to limit competition in exhibition and cause difficulties for other chains' minicircuits and independent theatre owners. The last two are then vulnerable to buy-outs and takeovers. The resulting impact is that a few companies are allowed to get bigger and bigger by swallowing up smaller, innovative enterprises.
By the way, this also hits our consumers who are captive to the promotion which can be put on these larger chains and which are often not equally accessible across our lands. 1 think it is wonderful that Golden Agers can, I believe, either Tuesday night or Wednesday night, go to all the films and cinema they wish for $2.50, if they live in the major centres. But what about those who live in the hinterland where there are no such theatres? The film industry identified the problem with concentration in the film industry. It felt that this was a problem because significant competition is essential to a healthy and orderly market-place and therefore recommended that the Government take the necessary steps to prevent and eliminate any vertical integration of distribution and exhibition which would limit competition and restrain trade in the Canadian film industry.
Not only in the film industry do we find examples of concentration of ownership and power. The Canadian broadcasting industry is currently seeing firsthand the old bugaboo of corporation ownwership in broadcasting and cross-ownership in broadcasting, newspapers and electronic media. In a current case before the Canadian CRTC, arguments are being presented over whether the Power Corporation of Canada, a large and diversified holding company, will be granted permission to buy Tele-Metropole Incorporated. If that deal is approved, we will see Montreal's largest French language newspaper, La Presse, which owns as well three other daily newspapers in the province, eight weekly publications and a radio station, now take over a major television network. I would suggest that this is of serious concern. This application would have been virtually unthinkable in the days of the Kent Commission in the early 1980s. I believe that is the most striking example of a new era of deal making in the communications industry. We are as well witnessing other media magnates such as the Bassett and Eaton families of Baton Broadcasting and Allan Waters of Chum Ltd. who are getting into the act and expanding their operations through acquisition. This is totally unacceptable and leads me to believe that power tends to connect and absolute power connects absolutely.
The Conservative Government signalled support for such concentration and cross-media ownership last May by cancelling, without so much as a whisper, a former 1982 cabinet directive that the CRTC prevent cross-ownership. The
April 8, 1986

directive, I believe, was applied only once in its short life in a 1983 case involving the broadcasting licence of New Brunswick's Irving family. Its request for cross-media ownership was turned down, in essence, because it would have allowed too high a concentration of power in the communications field. The question was, basically, how much one owns of what is available. In this instance, there was very high concentration of ownership in a small area.
Last September the Conservatives dropped the Liberal directive and the CTRC now has the authority to allow K. C. Irving and his sons to control newspapers, television and radio stations in New Brunswick. I was tempted to show you a list of their holdings, Mr. Speaker, but I decided that it was not such a good idea. It is just that it does create a certain series of problems when one looks at competition and control.
David McKendry, a regulatory industries analyst with the Consumers' Association of Canada, said that the Irving decision, "was as good as telling the industry that cross-media ownership is fine and this Government is not concerned about it". But we have to be concerned about every-day Canadians and their right to unbiased information with such a concentration as that of the Irving family and, potentially, the Power Corporation, which has significant and diverse holdings not only in the media industry but also in other fields which require the free investigative powers of journalists and the electronic media to ensure coverage of vital issues with a relevantly unjaundiced eye. The Power Corporation and the Irving family can assure and reassure us over and over again that they do not interfere in the editorial policy. Perhaps they do not and perhaps they have no intention of doing so. But they may not always be the owners of these mechanisms of communication and who knows what the other corporate takeover entity might do and what the impact would be on journalistic independence. When it comes to the power of the pocketbook, there is every possibility that the media would remain silent and compromise journalistic freedom for the sake of their pay cheques from those it is protecting.
In summation, access by the Canadian public to the media and to the theatre is an important element of social and cultural enrichment. By ensuring free competition, we are allowing small enterprises to flourish and at present, with such a large emphasis on employment, I would think that the Government would understand it is in small business that employment is created and thus strengthen this Bill even further to disallow such concentrations of ownership.
In relation to cultural industries, we are very concerned with two areas which are of importance with respect to Bill C-91, that is the abuse of the dominant position and mergers. The Liberal Party is concerned about the abuse of dominant position provisions because Bill C-91 has added a new requirement concerning the object of the practice. This in effect becomes an additional test and renders proof more difficult. How will we be able to prevent film, cable and book distribution from abusing the dominant position?
Competition Tribunal Act
[ Translation]
Mr. Speaker, all this may seem very technical, and that is why I am now going to talk about the provisions regarding mergers involving cultural industries. In fact, this is the Achilles heel of the present legislation, and it is quite easy to prove. Since 1910, there has been only one conviction under this section of the Act.

I think we have taken the right approach by transferring this matter from criminal to civil law. This Bill has been weakened considerably, if we consider that in Bill C-29 we took into account 12 factors in determining if the law had been breached. In Bill C-91 the following important factors have been left out: the size differential between the relevant business and its competitors; any history of anti-competitive behaviour; any likelihood that the merger will result in the removal of a vigorous and effective competitor; any evidence of intent to prevent or lessen competition; and the likelihood that the merger will stimulate competition.
In the field of telecommunications we will have to monitor competition policy carefully as we are faced with much new technology-the implications of satellites, fibre optics and cable. Therefore, I deplore that in Clause 65 of the Bill concerning criteria for evaluation of mergers the nature and extent of change and innovations in a relevant market will no longer be applicable. Consequently, in view of all this, Bill C-91 will not be as effective for cultural industries because it does not address mergers on as wide a criteria base as is needed for these industries. They have either been diluted or removed.

I have to challenge the priorities of the Bill's objectives. In fact, I think it is clear that this Government is too concerned about economic efficiency at the national and international levels, so much so that it seems to have lost its perspective and completely forgotten the consumer. A striking example is the difficulty third parties will have in gaining access to the Competition Tribunal, which also goes to show how little consideration the consumer is given in this legislation.

I would like to finish by asking the same question as was asked by Adam Smith. "Is... improvement in the circumstances of the lower ranks of the people to be regarded as an advantage or as an inconvenience to the society?"
Perhaps we might all feel that this Bill will improve upon the existing legislation-it will. However, it might not be what we want. We should seek to improve the circumstances of the greater number of Canadians who are at a disadvantage when there is little competition in the market-place. In this case I stress the importance of the circumstances of the greater number of Canadian consumers of cultural goods.
Competition Tribunal Act

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask a question of the Hon. Member for Mount Royal (Mrs. Finestone). Given the fact that there is a provision in Bill C-91 which provides the Government with a mechanism to deal with the problems in the film industry when competition is unduly lessened, why will the Hon. Member not support the Bill?

Mr. Speaker, if my colleague thinks that I said I would not support the Bill then I regret that. I started my remarks by saying that it is a good Bill but that it needs some improvement. I said that this was the time for change and that the time had come. I said that 1 welcomed the Bill. What I pointed out was the removal of certain constraints and measures which would be used to evaluate mergers. That was my concern.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in the Hon. Member's remarks with respect to the film industry, what is it that bothers her with respect to the idea that integration vertically in the film industry would create a lack of competition? How would she stiffen up that provision?

Mr. Speaker, I was referring to the factors which have been left out. I would be appreciative if members of the committee would reconsider these factors when the Bill is being studied. I suggest members of the committee look at Bill C-29 and compare it to Bill C-91. In so doing, they will see that the factors which are left out are of concern, particularly with respect to all cultural industries where the distribution of films and books, et cetera, are key factors. The size differential between the relevant businesses of the parties to the merger and their competitors is a key issue, particularly here in Canada where our industries are smaller and must face the large American competitors coming into the country.
If the Hon. Member recalls, yesterday I asked where the criteria of Investment Canada begin and end in terms of this Bill. I think there is an overlapping of jurisdictions which needs some clarification, particularly with respect to that factor. Also, any history of anti-competitor behaviour on the part of any party must be considered. I do not want to name names but I can tell Hon. Members that there is a fine history of anti-competitive behaviour in Canada. The report with respect to France Film which is before Hon. Members is good proof of that. The report deals with Cineplex Odeon, Famous Players and France Film. Cineplex Odeon brought the complaint before it was joined by Odeon and the Rank firm. I think it is quite relevant.
Another factor which has been left out of Bill C-91 is with respect to any likelihood that the merger will result in the removal of a vigorous and effective competitor. Then there is the factor dealing with any evidence of intent to prevent or lessen competition. There is also the factor with respect to any
April 8, 1986
likelihood that the merger will result in a substantial foreclosure of sources of products or distributors. I would ask the Hon. Member to take a look at what is happening in the book publishing and distribution industry and what happened to a number of booksellers which we have out in the market-place.
There is another factor with respect to the nature and extent of change and innovation in the relevant market. I would ask the Hon. Member to look at what is happening in the cable and satellite industries and to consider the fact that technology is changing at such a rapid pace. How can we measure if we do not have a measuring stick in place when looking at mergers? It is very important.
Then there is the likelihood that the merger will stimulate competition. This is another factor which I think should be taken into consideration.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to point out a few things to the Hon. Member. When talking about Bill C-29 we are talking about a Bill which was not enacted. It was a Bill of the former Government. We have been talking about these types of Bills for 16 years now. We have been dealing with competition legislation which has been in place for some 75 years.
Let us consider the five points which the Hon. Member has mentioned. First, this Bill strengthens rather than weakens or lessens control in the following ways. The maximum fine for conspiracy is increased up to $5 million from considerably less than that in the previous Government's Bill. The Hon. Member spoke about lessening competition. The "test in merger" which we are using states "lessen competition substantially". The test that would have been used by the Hon. Member's Party was to "lessen competition significantly". The Hon. Member can play on words all she wants. When we talk about competition and substantial reductions in it there are more teeth contained in the word "significantly" than were contained in Bill C-29. The thresholds for pre-notification have been reduced. In Bill C-29 one had to acquire a company in excess of $70 million. That was the threshold. In Bill C-91 it has only to be in excess of $35 million for investigation, prenotification and a hearing before the tribunal to take place.
As admitted by the Consumers' Association of Canada in its press releases, the setting up of a competition tribunal is a strengthening of the legislation. It is pleased to see Bill C-91 allowing a tribunal to investigate mergers which might create a lessening of competition. Finally, the investigative powers of the director of investigations and research are made more effective in conformity with the Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
With these five strengthening provisions that we can use to get at mergers which reduce competition in the market-place, I think that the Hon. Member would be anxious to see not only some ideas of the former Government put in place but some strengthening ideas which have been included in Bill C-91. The sooner we get the matter to committee the sooner we can call all the witnesses the Hon. Member would like to hear from

April 8, 1986

and the sooner we can bring the legislation back for third reading. A great many mergers which have taken place in the last 20 years have taken place because no Government has brought in any legislation with any teeth in it to stop what the Hon. Member wants to have stopped.

Mr. Speaker, first, I appreciate the Hon. Member bringing these points to my attention. I am delighted that the Government has taken into consideration Bill C-29. It is not interfering by filibustering as Members opposite did when they were in opposition when Bill C-29 was before the House. At that time they rang the bells and made life very difficult for a Party that was in a minority position. We are responding in the way that we must respond. We are pleased that there is now a position of dominance, perhaps, which is covered in the Bill. Therefore, we will not be subject to the harassments and pressures of big business. We will not cave in. Further, we will support the Government's efforts in this regard. I would like to suggest that the Government review some of the defences since fines are not enough. By the time we get around to imposing fines the damage is sometimes irreversible.

Mr. Speaker, I too wish to say a few words on the principle behind Bill C-91, the amendment to the Combines Investigation Act. I have been here since 1968 and I can recall many times when attempts were made to bring combines legislation into the House. In fact, if my memory serves me correctly, this is the sixth time legislation has been proposed to amend the Combines Investigation Act.
Way back in 1969, the Economic Council of Canada did a study and recommended that we needed a stronger combines legislation to provoke more genuine competition in the marketplace. As a result of that, a whole string of Bills were introduced starting with Bill C-2 back in 1971 and then moving on to Bill C-256, Bill C-42, Bill C-13, Bill C-29 and now Bill C-91.
I see we have a new Speaker in the House. I would like to commend you on your new position, Mr. Speaker. You look very distinguished sitting in that chair. I am sure that your constituents in The Battlefords-Meadow Lake will be very proud. There is no increase in pay, by the way.
This is the sixth attempt to amend the competition legislation in Canada. I suppose the only positive thing we can say about this Bill is that it will probably pass. It is better than the others and so it will pass. In the past, tremendous business lobbies have persuaded various Ministers of previous Liberal Governments to withdraw legislation, sometimes in a minority Government and sometimes in a majority Government. However, in all cases the business lobby was very powerful and well financed and hired efficient PR people. These lobbyists persuaded parliamentarians to withdraw the legislation.
Competition Tribunal Act
The legislation we have today is in many ways still very much of a toothless tiger, as our critic, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow), has said. As reported on page 11935 of Hansard, he said:
If we are going to be fair, we must say that this Bill is better than its predecessor. I say that only because the legislation we have had until now has proven completely useless. Previous Bills have failed to do anything to control mergers or see that we have any real competition.
The Bill that we are dealing with today is in many ways like a toothless old hound dog and one reason for that is that, as I understand it, the advisory committee to the Minister included five very powerful groups that were in the same ball park regarding their interests. Those groups were the Business Council on National Issues, a very powerful lobbying group with a certain point of view; the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, a very large business group with a certain point of view; and the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, again a business group representing large manufacturing firms with a certain point of view that is not unlike the point of view of the two previous groups. As well, there was the Grocery Products Manufacturers of Canada Association, again an organization of business types with a very similar point of view to that of the Chamber of Commerce, the Manufacturers' Association and the Council on National Issues. These four groups come from the same general sector of Canadian society in terms of outlook, interests and ideology. They were joined by the Canadian Bar Association, not a business organization but a fairly conservative, staid type of organization.
[ Translation]
I am sure the Hon. Member from Quebec agrees with me. He is entirely in agreement, because these five organizations are even too conservative for the Conservative Member from Quebec, because he is a red Tory, a Conservative who is more progressive than his Minister.

What is the definition of a red Tory?
The meaning of red.

I am asked about the meaning of a red Tory. I am sorry that you are in the chair, Mr. Speaker. Perhaps you could define that better than I. I was here for many years with John Diefenbaker. His riding bordered yours, Mr. Speaker, and was not too far from mine. He was a good example of a red Tory in certain ways, as was Robert Stanfield. There have been a few members of the Conservative Party who at times have been more progressive than Liberals.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I'm not going over with you guys, I can tell you that.

Well, John, you are progressing. You moved from the Liberals to the Conservatives. By the time you're 50, you will probably be here.
The reason this Bill is so conservative is that these five groups were on the advisory committee. I am very curious about this fact. I have nothing against the Chamber of Commerce or the Canadian Manufacturers' Association. In fact, there have been New Democratic Party Governments in Manitoba, Saskatchewan and British Columbia that have had advisory committees composed of Chambers of Commerce and manufacturing groups, but while these people were on their advisory groups, there were also representatives of trade unions or farm organizations, consumer groups, academic groups, women's organizations and community groups.
It seems to be fairly strange that we have a relatively new Government and a new Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) who has spent much time criticizing the old Party of the Minister of Justice, the Liberal Party, for being very centralist and for being controlled by the bureaucracy and a few people within the Prime Minister's Office rather than listening to the people of Canada. The Conservatives said that they would open up the Government. To use the words of a former Prime Minister, Conservatives said that there would be more participatory democracy and openness in this Government. Yet on the drafting of a very important piece of legislation, farmers and fishermen were not represented nor were consumers or ordinary Canadians.
I am sure that if you were not in that chair, Mr. Speaker, you would be making a speech about how concerned you are that your constituents like mine have been frozen out from representing their views on this committee that advised the Minister when he drafted the new competition legislation. In a democracy, it is very important that advisory groups to Ministers who are members of any Party be reflective of the country as a whole, but this did not happen in this case. That is one reason why this legislation is acceptable to big business. That is one reason why big business is not fighting this legislation. Big business is getting about 90 per cent, if not more, of what it wanted from the Conservative Government.
I would like to make only one point and that is that we need much stronger legislation. Our Party has been consistent on that point. The Hon. Member for Winnipeg North, our spokesman, has outlined the different things he would like to see changed in this particular Bill. He has mentioned legislation that he would like to see strengthened. I hope that when this Bill gets to committee stage, there will be a broad cross section of Canadians who will come before the committee to tell us what they want in a competition policy for Canada. We
need a competition policy. We need legislation to make sure that companies do not form monopolies or oligopolies or become monstrous giants that gouge, steal from and pick the pockets of ordinary Canadians.
Before I sit down this afternoon, I would like to tell the House of one example of an industry in which there is, in my opinion, a near monopoly created because of a lack of legislation. Here I am not criticizing the Conservative Government because it has only been in office for 18 months. I am talking about farm chemical companies. In Canada, there are a few farm chemical companies, almost all of which are owned by Americans or foreign companies. These companies sell chemicals to Canadian farmers and they have a monopoly on their patents of 17 years once the chemicals are registered.
When looking at the price of chemicals in Canada, one sees that farmers are being gouged. They are paying excessive rates for farm chemicals. The reason I mention this now is that it is so relevant to the question of competition. I think Parliament should pass a law to provide for generic farm chemicals just like the one that provides for generic pharmaceuticals. If a chemical company develops a new chemical at the present time, it has a 17-year exclusive monopoly on the sale and production of that chemical in Canada. There can be no competition whatsoever under Canadian law. That is not good enough. It is particularly not good enough in a Parliament which is discussing competition policy.
I should like to put a few facts on the record about farm chemicals as an example of why we need stronger competition policy. A survey was conducted recently by the Manitoba Institute of Agrologists for the Senate Committee on Agriculture. The Senate is a fairly staid and conservative institution.
Sometimes.

It has become radical in recent weeks, but it was a fairly conservative and staid institution before that time. The Manitoba Institute of Agrologists indicated that the price of active ingredients in a sample of non-patented herbicides averaged $2.96 per pound while a sample of patented herbicides showed a price of $29.67 per pound. On average it was 10 times as high. When active ingredient chemicals were off patent, the price was one-tenth of the price of chemicals under exclusive patents held by multinational companies.
Let us look at the price of Round-up, which is produced by a company called Monsanto. By the way, Monsanto is a very large multinational company which produces a chemical used very widely in your province, Mr. Speaker, as well as in mine. The company is foreign owned. It has an exclusive 17-year patent on the product called Round-up. According to a study conducted by Merrill Lynch, a very renowned stockbrokerage firm, in June, 1982, the market share for Round-up was 100 per cent controlled by Monsanto because there was no competition. The Round-up sales in 1982 amounted to $472 million. Its gross profit margin was 75 per cent, and its gross
April 8, 1986

profits were $357 million. Its net income was $181 million and the earnings per share were about $4.50. Let us refer to the projected market share, the projected earnings and sales of the Monsanto product, Round-up, according to Merrill Lynch. From 1982 to 1988 it will keep 100 per cent of the market because it has an exclusive patent for the product. No competition will be allowed under Canadian law. The company will have that exclusive right. The $472 million of sales in 1982 will go up to $1 billion in 1988 according to the projection. Also we see the net income of the company going up from $180 million to $333 million, guaranteed by the law. We see the profit or the earnings per share going up from $4.50 to $8.25, again guaranteed by the law. It is an example of why we should not only look at competition policy but at the patent laws as well. However, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Cote) is now entertaining the thought of perhaps changing the generic pharmaceutical legislation to allow for an exclusive patent once again as was the case prior to 1970. That is a backward step, a step toward giving more and more power to fewer and fewer people who control pharmaceuticals in Canada.
Returning to Monsanto for a few moments, I know the Parliamentary Secretary is not a westerner and is not as familiar with some of these terms. Round-up is a very important chemical for farmers. The evidence before the Senate Committee on Agriculture indicated that the price of Roundup in Canada was sitting at $24 per litre. However, the price in Australia was some $17 per litre, again according to the study by Merrill Lynch. The price is about 40 per cent higher in Canada despite the fact that it is 9,000 miles closer to the source where Round-up is produced. Round-up is patented in both countries, but for marketing purposes it is sold for a lower price by Monsanto in Australia. In fact, in order to indicate the size of the particular company, its development costs are about $40 million, and these costs are recovered every 24 days through the company's sales around the world. Every 24 days it sells enough chemicals to make up its development costs of some $40 million. This powerful, multinational company is gouging farmers by charging excessive rates for its farm chemicals. However, in Australia, where the stuff has to be shipped an extra 9,000 miles, the company charges 40 per cent less.
There is something wrong with our laws when we as parliamentarians allow that kind of situation to occur in Canada. That is why we should not be afraid of big companies and should be drafting tougher laws when it comes to competition, patents, generics and such things.
I should like to refer to a few more examples of what I mean. There is a chemical called Atrazine which is used out West on rape-seed and in central Canada on corn. Perhaps the Hon. Member for Peterborough (Mr. Domm) will be more familiar with that particular chemical. Atrazine dopped by about 30 per cent in price from the late 1970s despite inflation because it came off patent. In the late 1970s the price of Atrazine was $43.50 for a 10-litre jug. The price after patent
Competition Tribunal Act
in 1984 dropped down to $30 for the same 10-litre jug, a drop of some 30 per cent, without even taking inflation into account. It was because it came off patent and there was some competition for the particular product. It is a good example of what can happen when there is more competition in the marketplace and what can happen when a certain company has a monopoly. It is a good example to use when discussing the principles of the Bill before us, why the Bill should be strengthened and why good competition legislation is needed in Canada.
There are various other examples one could use. The Hon. Member for Winnipeg North recently spoke in the House about generic pharmaceuticals. In 1969, when I first came down here, I recall that there was legislation before the House to end the exclusive 17-year patents for pharmaceutical companies. They were ended and, as a result, we have found that pharmaceutical prices dropped significantly compared with those in the United States. In fact, the Eastman Report indicated that the average price of chemicals in Canada in 1969 was about 9 per cent higher than the price in the United States. By 1976, after we had generic pharmaceuticals for a few years, the average price of pharmaceuticals in Canada was 21 per cent lower than the price in the United States. In fact, there was a time when Hoffman-Laroche was so determined to stop copies of its popular tranquillizer, Valium, from getting into hospitals that it gave away Valium to hospitals for one year. That just shows the size of the company and the assets it has to promote its tranquillizer, Valium. It is another good example of why we need strong competition legislation. If we do not have it, farmers and consumers will pay much more than they should for the various products they must buy.
The reason I have used farm chemicals as an example this afternoon is that I come from a farm riding. Because of the economic situation in the world today, I know that the income of farmers is going down. The price of grain is also down. The Americans have a farm Bill which is very protectionistic. It will drive the price of wheat down by another 20 per cent to 25 per cent, according to the federal Government. Also there has been a drought on the Prairies. On the other side of the ledger, there has been a tremendous increase in input costs for products such as fertilizers and up until recently fuel costs. By the way, the price of diesel is still not tracking its way down, as it should. However, one large input cost is that of farm chemicals. In my remaining minute let me say that in 1984 the Canadian farm chemical business had sales of $778 million, three-quarters of $1 billion. It is a big industry and there are big rip-offs, Mr. Speaker. In fact, there is a gentleman named Mr. Gawdy, who you may know, at Melfort who is trying to set up a company in competition with some of these huge multinationals. He could sell farm chemicals 20 per cent, 30 per cent, probably 50 per cent or 60 per cent cheaper to farmers in our province if we had a change in the patent laws and in the product specification Act of this country. Not only Mr. Gawdy, but the co-operatives, the wheat pools, the provincial wheat pools, provincial Governments or the federal Government or joint ventures between all sorts of people can

April 8, 1986

produce farm chemicals at a much cheaper rate. We can produce a lot more at a much cheaper rate in this country.
I make an appeal to this House to make sure, when the Bill goes to committee, that we strengthen the legislation, that we get input from more than just the big business community and big business concerns and that we have some genuine competition legislation. Later on we should amend the Patent Act so that we can get farm chemicals and other products to ordinary Canadians at a price that is reasonable so that they can carry on their livelihood and make a contribution to this great country of Canada.

interests and the Canadian Bar Association. I do not think that is good enough.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think I should clear up the misconception that in the West and in the area of Saskatchewan and other prairie provinces as well as in British Columbia there was more than just correspondence in the form of consultation. I was part of a group, including the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Cote) who went to the western provinces and met with Ministers of Consumer and Commercial Relations in the provinces. I think they are well able and capable of speaking for consumers in the various provinces. We met with them, we discussed our intent as it pertains to competition legislation. We heard their input. If that is not good enough, I am sure the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) will know someone in his area who is a member of the Canadian Federation of Independent Petroleum marketers, not big corporations but independent marketers across this country, and we had full consultation with them.
To add to that, there must be people in Saskatchewan who belong to organizations like the Canadian Federation of Labour. We had correspondence directly with its President. He had dialogued directly with officials within the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. It was at his urging in large measure that we incorporated into Bill C-91 the provision for the tribunal. He liked it.
I am sure the President represents a lot of labour in the province not only in Saskatchewan but in other provinces as well. There was consultation with organizations like the Canadian Federation of Independent Businessmen, one of the largest national organizations representing businesses doing less than $2 million a year, and 100 representations were made to the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and the Minister directly so I fail to see that there has not been a broad range of consultation and a general consensus that this Bill is urgently needed. I have yet to hear from anyone who does not want the Bill to proceed to committee directly. If there is some fine tuning, that is the place to do it, not by taking up too much time in this House.

Mr. Speaker, the Parliamentary Secretary mentioned the Canadian Federation of Labour. It is indeed very small in Saskatchewan. Most of our people are affiliated with the Canadian Labour Congress.
The Parliamentary Secretary was very careful to say that there was full consultation with all these groups by himself or the Minister, that there was correspondence with a whole
April 8, 1986

series of organizations and individuals, and that' there was dialogue with all kinds of different people concerned about this Bill. These are words I heard from Liberal Governments year in and year out: dialogue, correspondence, communication and so on.
Is it or is it not the case that there was an advisory committee and that the advisory committee consisted of the Business Council on National Issues, the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, the Grocery Products Manufacturers of Canada and the Canadian Bar Association? The Parliamentary Secretary nods.
I have been around the workings of Parliament and Government long enough to know that when there is an advisory council, that council usually has an awful lot of influence. Often when you consult other groups that are not on the advisory council, it is window dressing, it is lip service.
I could probably go through Hansard and dig out speeches which the Hon. Member for Peterborough made when he was on this side of the House in which he said similar kinds of things. The Liberal Parliamentary Secretary would get up and say "Well, we consulted the farmers or the NFU. We consulted the steelworkers of America" and so on. The important thing is who is appointed to the advisory council.
Four business groups and one group of lawyers who represent the business groups were appointed. We have business groups and their lawyers advising the Minister on this issue. That is the point I made. I do not see that as having real input from various groups. Sure you can get a letter from the Consumers' Association of Canada. You can call up that Association and ask for advice. You can dialogue a little bit if you want with the President of the National Farmers Union or someone else. Why not put representatives of the farming community on the advisory committee? Why not put representatives of the labour movement on the advisory committee? Why not put some consumer representatives on the advisory committee? Why not put someone from the Status of Women or the Action Committee on the Status of Women on the advisory committee?
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, if you want to have a truly representative piece of legislation, that is where you put them. These advisory committees have a lot of influence. They are the ones who tend to have more expertise, who tend to dialogue with experts in the area and who tend to have the ear of the Minister. Maybe this Parliamentary Secretary did an awful lot of consulting on his own. I do not try to pretend that he did not, but it is a lot easier to be consulted in a genuine way if you are a member of the advisory committee. Perhaps I could ask why this was not done.

Mr. Speaker, today I also have a few comments to make on Bill C-91, and I may say that the Liberal Party of Canada feels that sound competition legislation is necessary to ensure genuine competition on the Canadian market. -a branch of Gaz Metropolitain-
-Conversion Division, and especially Real Lefebvre and Sylvain Denis. I urge you to take action as soon as possible, if possible before Christmas. I want to be quite clear about the following items-

Mr. Speaker, here is one of thousands of small business people who are always struggling against the competition. Even if we do get through Bill C-91 today, this is not going to solve any of their problems.

There is also a letter written to one of my colleagues by a wholesaler, and I would also like to quote a few passages, for the record, so that Members will realize that there is competition and very strong competition at that, between small businesses and large businesses. And when Government Members stand up in the House to say that a Bill like C-91 helps small businesses, that is just not the case, and this letter emphasizes the fact it is not, although the Government would have us think otherwise.
1 quote a letter from W. A. MacLeod & Son Ltd:
The danger we face as wholesalers comes in the form of large anti-competitive conglomerates who threaten to damage us irreparably by marshalling their economic might against us. Their tactic is loss leader selling. Because of their huge size, they can sustain temporary losses. Slowly but surely, the use of this tactic can drive us out of business.

Mr. Speaker, we know very well-we often see advertisements-I see my colleague from Dollard (Mr. Weiner), a former drugstore owner who surely had such experiences-as I was saying, we often see cartons of cigarettes advertised at below cost price to attract customers. This Bill will do nothing to remedy that situation. Hopefully we will be able to get a closer look at that in committee, because it is now a problem for small businessmen and no independent storer owner can face that kind of competition. I continue quoting the letter:

Never before has the threat been as great. With the recent spate of mergers between large companies, the critical balance between big and small businesses could be irredeemably tipped towards the huge conglomerates. If their unreasonable and unfair practices go unchecked, the economy could be severely crippled. Wholesaling will become dominated by very few large sellers who will each have an entire market to themselves.
As with my fellow NATCD members, all the profits from my company remain in this locality. As an independent entrepreneur, I am part of the backbone of a healthy economy. In this age of rapid change, Canadian business needs all the imagination, flexibility and entrepreneurship it can muster.
As the owner of a small wholesaling business, I can be more responsive to changes in the business climate than a large bureaucratic, centrally located conglomerate.
Some examples of such business in direct competition with us. TRA Wholesale owned by the Sobey's group, Mason's Wholesale owned by Bolands Ltd. would operate IGA Supermarkets. Another serious threat to us in this area is Atlantic Wholesalers owned by Loblaws who are not yet in the area, but there have been rumours of this for some time now. Ever since TRA Wholesale have moved into Sydney, we have watched our profit margins on confectionery drastically decline. They regularly practise the use of "loss-leaders" and you and I know they can afford to. However, as a small independent wholesaler, I cannot.
On November 18, 1985, the NATCD President, Bill Marcus, wrote to the ... Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, requesting an amendment to the Combines Investigation Act to prohibit loss leader selling. The Minister in his reply of December 11, 1985 recognized our concerns:
I appreciate how damaging below cost pricing can be when it is engaged in for the purpose of lessening competition or eliminating competitors from the market.
Nevertheless, the Minister's full response was less than satisfactory. He considered it not appropriate to legislate an outright prohibition against loss leading pricing, suggesting that his forthcoming proposals to amend the Act (subsequently introduced in the House on December 17, 1985) would enable
Competition Tribunal Act
competition law to deal more effectively with predatory conduct through a new civil provision dealing with abuse of dominant position, to be adjudicated by a new Competition Tribunal.
I could continue because there are another two pages to the letter, but let me just say that small business is simply asking for a competition law with teeth. We must be able to stop some unscrupulous big businesses who are trying to take away the markets of small business which create most of the jobs in the local community. I do not see anywhere in this Bill that such protection can be achieved. Therefore, once this Bill moves to committee I hope Members will look into these details and make sure that all small business and consumer groups have their say. Then, when the Bill comes back to the House for third reading or clause-by-clause study, we can make sure that we have a competition law with enough teeth to protect consumers and small business.
Another example of what we can deal with under this legislation is the crisis in the liability insurance business. We had to ask the Minister to intervene in this situation, and when he did not we had to use the law to get an inquiry. We are still waiting for an answer and this is a problem which has to be solved. Then we have the Gulf refinery closing in the east end of Montreal. One company threatened to close its refinery and leave Quebec if another refinery was sold to someone else and remained open. This is the kind of situation we have to deal with today. We have to solve this problem once and for all and make sure that everyone in Canada is allowed to do business without being pushed around.
